name: Sara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the lettings side at a small independent agency on the high street of a market town, with two juniors under me. Mornings are rent arrears, repair calls and landlords ringing about their boiler. Afternoons I'm out doing viewings and check-ins with a clipboard and my phone camera. I love the tenants who finally get a decent place, and I'm worn out by landlords who treat a damp flat like a cash machine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep track of it all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paper diary, a wall planner and the office system we've had since before I joined. My manager Graham keeps telling me to try the AI tool that writes property adverts, but I write every advert myself. I know every street in this town and I'd rather a tenant read my words than a robot's. I'm the one who gets called when a tenant is crying on the phone, and no software is taking that call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: it's mostly a gimmick. The adverts it writes all sound the same, with every flat being bright and airy. At work I'd tell the juniors not to rely on it, because tenants can tell. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem in renting was never a lack of technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job stays, but my money problems don't go anywhere. I'm on lower pay than agents in the city and I've got less than a month's rent saved. Tom and I pay nine hundred a month for a flat above a launderette, and the landlord already hinted at a rise in spring. So AI fizzling out doesn't fix the thing that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it, and push Graham again for the pay review he promised last January. I'd put thirty pounds a week aside, even if it means fewer takeaways. I'd also go to the renters' union meeting in the library next month, because I've been meaning to for a year. That's about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI part, and a bit tired about everything else. Hearing AI fizzled out is like being told the storm missed you while you're still standing in a leaky house. I'm not panicking, but I'm not relaxed either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent rise in spring. What happens if it comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Tom and I are looking at the one-bed flats on my own books, which is a strange feeling. I've showed people round those flats and thought, glad that's not me. If it's more than fifty pounds, something has to give, probably his car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine tasks AI does take over don't touch you. Is any of your day routine screen work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, if I'm honest. Rent reminders and booking gas safety checks are dull and repetitive. If the office system started sending those itself, I'd grumble, but it wouldn't cost me my job. It'd just give me fewer excuses to avoid the landlords.

say: AI is mostly a **gimmick**, and tenants can tell when an advert was written by software.
The real problem in renting was never **technology**; it was rents and landlords.
think: My **job is safe**, but my pay is low and I have less than a month saved.
A **rent rise** in spring worries me more than any software ever has.
do: **Push** my manager for the **pay review** promised last January.
Put **thirty pounds** a week aside, even if it means fewer takeaways.
Go to the **renters' union** meeting at the library next month.
feel: **Relieved** that AI fizzled out, but **tired** of money worries that were already there.
S0.quote: Hearing AI fizzled out is like being told the storm missed you while you're still standing in a leaky house.
fieldNote: She frames AI as a **side issue**; rent and pay are the pressures she already carries.
Her refusal to use AI is about **pride in writing** and knowing every street, not fear.
Interesting **irony**: she may end up renting a flat from her own books.

steps.text: Ask Graham for the overdue pay review before Christmas
Save thirty pounds a week by cutting takeaways
Join the renters' union branch that meets at the library

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say agencies are using AI to cut corners and cut staff, and tenants will pay for it. When a pipe bursts at midnight, a chatbot won't come round with towels. Online I'd back anyone pushing for rules so tenants always get a real person. At work I'd be the one at the meeting asking who loses their hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of what I do is exactly that list: writing adverts, checking references, booking contractors, answering tenants. The national portals already have chatbots that book viewings. If Graham can run lettings with one person and a computer, it won't be the expensive one he keeps. My two juniors go first, then they'll look at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally sit down with the AI tool, even though I hate it, because being the person who refuses is how you become the person who's let go. I'd cut our spending properly: Tom's car goes on the market by summer. I'd join the union for estate agency staff, which I've never bothered with. And I'd start looking at housing association jobs, because those are about people, not adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a slow way. Like watching the water rise an inch a month. I don't trust myself to learn the new systems quickly, and that's the bit that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your juniors would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kayleigh, who's nineteen and just moved out of her mum's. Her whole job is booking viewings and answering the phone, which is the first thing these tools do. I'd want to help her find something before the company decides for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tool even though you hate it. Which is stronger, the hate or the fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fear, if I'm truthful. I can be stubborn when there's a safety net. There isn't one here, not with less than a month saved and only three agencies in town.

say: Agencies are using AI to **cut staff**, and tenants will pay for it when things break.
Tenants should **always get** a real person, and I'd back rules that make that happen.
think: Most of my desk work is on that list: **adverts, references** and bookings.
My **juniors go first**, and then the company will look at my salary.
do: **Learn** the AI advert tool, even though I hate it, so I'm not the one who refused.
**Sell** Tom's car by summer to cut our monthly costs.
**Join** the estate agency union and start looking at **housing association** jobs.
feel: **Scared** in a slow way, like water rising an inch a month.
Worried I'm **too slow** with new systems to keep up.
S1.quote: When a pipe bursts at midnight, a chatbot won't come round with towels.
fieldNote: Her **public line** is about tenants; her private fear is about her own salary.
She'll adapt only under **pressure**: thin savings remove the option to be stubborn.
She worries about her junior Kayleigh before herself, a sign of **team lead** loyalty.

steps.text: Practise with the AI advert tool on three listings a week
Sell Tom's car by summer to cut monthly costs
Join the estate agency staff union
Apply for housing association lettings jobs in the county

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being done to us, not with us, and nobody voted for it. At work I'd say we need the government to step in before agencies sack everyone. Online I'd be angry, and I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think lettings as a desk job is finished within two years. Everything I do from the office could be done by a computer by 2028. What's left is the in-person stuff: check-ins, inventories, standing in a cold flat with a tenant. That buys me maybe three years until the robots come, and only if Graham still needs a human face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the hands-on side straight away: inventory clerk work, check-outs, property inspections. I'd ask Tom whether his mum would let us live in her spare room to save the rent. I'd apply for every government retraining grant going, probably for something like social care, where people still want people. And I'd go on the marches, because I'd want my voice somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me who doesn't pick things up quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we need to stop pretending we'll buy a house this decade. Then I'd probably cry, and he'd make tea, because that's what he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come three years later. Does that hands-on part feel like a real shelter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. Showing people round a house, noticing the mould behind the wardrobe, calming someone down in a doorway, that's hands-on. But I'd be one of a hundred agents fighting for those few jobs in a town with three agencies.

say: This is being **done to us**, and nobody voted for it.
The **government** must step in before agencies sack everyone.
think: Lettings as a **desk job** is finished within two years.
The **in-person** work buys me about three more years, if anyone still needs a human face.
do: **Move** into inventory and inspection work, the hands-on side of lettings.
**Ask** Tom's mum about her **spare room** to save our rent.
**Apply** for every retraining grant and go on the **marches**.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor has gone from under me.
Sure that two years is **not enough** for someone slow with technology.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for someone like me who doesn't pick things up quickly.
fieldNote: She sees the **hands-on** parts of lettings as a short shelter, not a real one.
Her **politics** turn from rules for tenants to protest for workers.
Moving in with Tom's mother shows how thin her **cushion** is.

steps.text: Ask Graham to move her into inventory and inspection work
Move into Tom's mum's spare room to stop paying rent
Apply for a government retraining grant in social care
March and sign petitions for protection for sacked workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. At work I'd say we should be sitting down now to plan who does what. I'd be loud about it at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lettings as a desk job is finished within two years, and I'm not someone who picks things up quickly. With five years it's 2031 instead, and maybe 2034 for the hands-on bits. That's enough time to get Tom and me into a better spot, but only if I actually start, and I'm terrible at starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the evening course in housing management at the college, the one that leads to a council job. I'd get the union to push Graham for a written plan for staff. I'd save every bonus instead of spending it on Christmas. And I'd keep doing my job, properly, because a good reference matters more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling and more like a deadline. I'd be anxious, but at least there's a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're terrible at starting. What would actually get you started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone booking it for me, honestly. If the union or the council said here's a course, Tuesday nights, it's paid for, I'd go. If I have to dig through websites, I'll put it off till it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a council job rather than another agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Councils still have to house people, and the work is checking on families and fixing things, not writing adverts. And I trust a public employer more than an agency owner, because Graham will sell the business the minute a portal offers him the right price.

say: Five years is a **warning**, and wasting it would be the government's fault.
Agencies and staff should be **planning now** about who does what.
think: 2031 gives Tom and me **time** to get somewhere better.
My real problem is **starting**, because I put things off.
do: **Sign up** for the evening course in **housing management** at the college.
**Push** the union to get a written staff plan from my manager.
**Save** every bonus instead of spending it at Christmas.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a **map** instead of a cliff edge.
S3.quote: Councils still have to house people, and the work is checking on families and fixing things, not writing adverts.
fieldNote: She repeats her line about **desk lettings** ending, showing the fast picture still frames her thinking.
She needs a **ready-made course** to move; her resistance is about starting, not ability.
She trusts **public employers** over agency owners.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening housing management course at the college
Ask the union to get a written staff plan from Graham
Put every bonus into savings instead of Christmas spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for chaos. I'd tell friends to train for something now while it's cheap and quiet. Online I'd push for the government to fund retraining for everyone, not just people in tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one where I'd waste time. I know myself. I'd tell myself 2036 is ages away, and I'd be thirty-seven before I noticed. But it does mean I'm not in my late twenties fighting for scraps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year and one task: get the housing management qualification. I'd keep my job and keep saving a little each month. And I'd talk to Tom about a long plan, maybe moving to the city where the council housing jobs are, around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, oddly, but a bit guilty at how calm. It's the same end, just further off, so I'd still feel it in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste time. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the diary. Tom is good at that, he plans the shopping a week ahead. If he says we're looking at council jobs in March, I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your rent and pay worries from the first picture, are they still there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. Ten years doesn't fix a landlord who wants another fifty pounds. I'd still be counting every month, just with a longer runway on the job side.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to do this fairly, so chaos would be inexcusable.
Government should fund **retraining for everyone**, not just people in tech.
think: I'd **waste the time** if I'm not careful, because 2036 sounds far away.
Rent and pay **pressures** stay with me whatever happens to AI.
do: **Finish** the housing management qualification within the first year.
**Keep** my job and keep saving a little each month.
**Plan** with Tom a possible **move** to the city around 2030.
feel: **Calmer**, but a bit **guilty** about feeling calm.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't fix a landlord who wants another fifty pounds.
fieldNote: The long runway lowers her fear about the job but not about **rent and pay**.
She relies on her partner Tom for **deadlines**, which she sees clearly in herself.
She stays **anxious** because her savings and local job options remain thin.

steps.text: Finish the housing management qualification within a year
Keep running lettings and save fifty pounds a month
Plan a move with Tom to the city for council jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years would catch me with no savings, no new skills and nowhere else in town to go. What would help is a paid course I don't have to hunt for, and some rule that agencies have to keep humans for tenants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but the people renting from us are the ones who'll be stuck talking to a machine about mould. I'd still fight for them, even if I'm not the one at the desk.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but the people renting from us are the ones who'll be stuck talking to a machine about mould.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old **lettings team lead** at a small market-town agency, living with her partner Tom.
She writes every advert herself and has **never used** AI tools, out of pride more than fear.
Her real pressures are **low pay**, less than a month saved and a landlord hinting at a rent rise.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, needing deadlines to act.
She sees **housing management** for a council as the safest place for her people skills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** would catch her with no savings, no new skills and nowhere else to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** she doesn't have to hunt for, booked for her.
Rules that agencies must keep **real people** for tenants.
